scopeReview: IMP-4.C.1 andIMP-4.D.1: federal versus unitary forms and their spatial power centers. Constitutional allocation is distinguished from delegated tasks, local office location, policy variation, national identity and regime type; tendencies are not deterministic guarantees.
varietyReview: Delegation network, constitutional comparison table, policy-target choropleth and multilevel-center map. Seven cases address Switzerland, unitary decentralization, accountability, shared resources, geographic motives, multinational identity and issue-specific authority. Four interpreted stimuli, all five skills and varied keys.
repetitionReview: Evidence distinguishes institutional structure from spatial indicators. Definition is applied through different settings rather than eleven labels; constitution examples remain broad, not jurisdiction-specific legal advice. No exact duplicate stem or numeric-only clone; difficulty uncalibrated.
referenceNote: Primary current institutional accounts checked. All diagrams, regions and percentages are original hypothetical examples; Switzerland’s classification is factual. No new approved resource or human-review claim; policies and powers are not generalized beyond stated assumptions.

questions.correctOption: The arrangement illustrates a unitary hierarchy with regional implementation of centrally derived authority.
questions.independentReview: Compared source of authority with physical office location. Central instructions alone could occur in multiple systems; the ordinary-law revocable delegation premise is what supports the unitary interpretation.

questions.correctOption: Case B, because its constitution protects authority for both national and regional governments.
questions.independentReview: Checked each case’s legal-institutional premise: A ordinary delegation, B constitutional allocation. The item does not claim every federal amendment requires identical consent rules or that regional powers are unlimited.

questions.correctOption: Constitutional information about regional authority, since policy variation alone does not establish a federal structure.
questions.independentReview: Verified the map displays targets40/60/40/60, not constitutional clauses or actual recycling outcomes. Variation is compatible with multiple arrangements, so the question does not infer federalism from an ecological indicator.

questions.correctOption: Constitutionally meaningful power centers can be distributed across regions alongside a national center.
questions.independentReview: Checked four regional centers plus one national center and explicitly supplied constitutional allocation. The map’s mere dots would be insufficient without that premise; no capital is inferred to control every matter.

questions.correctOption: A federal system can distribute authority among territorial levels while remaining one state.
questions.independentReview: Verified Switzerland’s current federal structure using its official2026 guide and constitutional framework. Did not repeat the inaccurate claim that every canton has two Council of States seats; representation details are outside this item.

questions.correctOption: A unitary state can decentralize tasks; the amount of local activity alone does not establish constitutionally federal authority.
questions.independentReview: Checked primary French institutional descriptions showing territorial administration/decentralization within a unitary state. No real local authority’s exact legal competence is generalized to every state.

questions.correctOption: Federal/unitary describes territorial allocation of authority, which does not by itself determine democratic accountability.
questions.independentReview: Independently separated territorial power allocation from regime/accountability type. No claim is made that either structure universally guarantees rights, efficiency, equality or legitimacy.

questions.correctOption: Use the constitutionally allocated responsibilities and intergovernmental procedures to address a cross-regional problem.
questions.independentReview: Checked physical interdependence against potentially shared or allocated authority. No uniform water-law rule is prescribed; the answer asks which institutional evidence and procedures are relevant.

questions.correctOption: Distance and regional differences can motivate dispersed authority, but do not uniquely determine the chosen system or its success.
questions.independentReview: Verified that the course describes tendencies in power organization, not a size threshold forcing federalism. The answer preserves institutional choice and possible coordination/resource constraints.

questions.correctOption: Multinational in its communities and unitary in its territorial allocation of authority.
questions.independentReview: Compared the4.1 entity dimension with the4.7 governance dimension. Centralization is explicitly supplied; no nation’s identity or constitutional status is inferred from a language or population share.

questions.correctOption: The constitution and relevant allocation of responsibilities for the particular policy issue.
questions.independentReview: Matched the specific policy question to actual allocated powers, not proximity or an unsupported all-issues assumption. This is an analytical research task, not advice about a real school’s legal options.
